## Spleen Examination ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ – General Surgery: Clinical Examination & OSCE Questions

- 2. Manoeuvres (Q2)

title: 1. Demonstrate palpation of the spleen
model_answer:
### Preparation

- Wash your hands.
- Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity.
- Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
- Ask about pain before starting.
- Expose the abdomen appropriately, from the xiphisternum to the pubic symphysis.
- Position the patient supine, with the head supported and knees slightly flexed.
- Stand on the patient's right side.

### Technique: Bimanual palpation (step-by-step)

- Place your left hand behind the patient's left lower rib cage, approximately over the 9th–11th ribs.
- Use your left hand to lift the lower rib cage anteriorly.
- Place your right hand flat on the abdomen, starting in the right iliac fossa (RIF).
- Position your fingers obliquely, pointing towards the left axilla.
- Ask the patient to take a deep breath in.
- During inspiration, the enlarged spleen descends and moves towards your fingertips.
- Feel for the splenic edge.
- During expiration, move your hand diagonally upwards towards the left hypochondrium.
- Repeat this process until you reach the left costal margin.

:::important Important
Always start in the right iliac fossa, not directly below the left costal margin. A massively enlarged spleen may extend all the way into the pelvis or even towards the right side of the abdomen.
:::

### What should you feel? (if the spleen is enlarged)

- A firm or soft mass descending during inspiration.
- A characteristic palpable notch on its medial border.
- A sharp or rounded edge.
- A smooth surface (although it can be irregular in certain pathologies).
- Movement with respiration.
- Tenderness if there is inflammation, infarction or an acute complication.

:::pearl Exam pearl
The splenic notch is an important distinguishing feature. You cannot get above an enlarged spleen because it extends underneath the left costal margin.
:::

:::reference Reference
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov +2
:::

title: How do you differentiate an enlarged spleen from an enlarged kidney?
model_answer:
| Feature | Spleen | Kidney |
|---|---|---|
| Notch | Usually present | Absent |
| Direction of enlargement | Downwards and medially | Downwards |
| Movement with respiration | Moves | Moves |
| Ballotability | Not ballotable | Ballotable |
| Getting above the mass | Impossible | Usually possible |
| Percussion | Dull | Usually resonant over anterior surface due to bowel |

:::pearl Exam pearl
The splenic notch is an important distinguishing feature. You cannot get above an enlarged spleen because it extends underneath the left costal margin.
:::

title: 2. What are the two manoeuvres for splenic palpation?
model_answer:
### Overview

There are two commonly taught approaches:

### A. Middleton's manoeuvre (hooking method)

- The examiner stands on the patient's left side.
- The fingers of the right hand are hooked underneath the left costal margin.
- Ask the patient to take a deep breath.
- Try to feel the descending splenic edge against your fingertips.

This is particularly useful when the spleen is only mildly enlarged.

### B. Nixon's manoeuvre (right lateral position)

- Position the patient in the right lateral decubitus position.
- Flex the left hip and knee slightly.
- Stand behind the patient.
- Place your left hand behind the left lower ribs.
- Palpate the left upper abdomen with your right hand.
- Ask the patient to breathe deeply.

### Principle (Nixon's)

Gravity brings the spleen more anteriorly and closer to the examining hand, making it easier to detect mild splenomegaly.

:::important Important distinction for your viva
Some teaching sources describe the two manoeuvres as the bimanual (standard) method and Middleton's hooking method. Nixon's manoeuvre is another recognized technique, particularly in the right lateral position. Therefore, clarify which classification your examiner expects.
:::

:::reference Reference
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov +2
:::

title: 3. What are the causes of splenomegaly?
model_answer:
### Approach

The best way to answer this in an examination is to classify the causes into groups.

## A. Hematological causes (particularly important)

### 1. Hemolytic anemias

- Hereditary spherocytosis.
- Thalassemia.
- Sickle cell disease (particularly HbSC and some other sickle syndromes; advanced HbSS often causes autosplenectomy).
- Autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
- G6PD deficiency (especially with ongoing or recurrent hemolysis).

### 2. Hematological malignancies

- Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
- Acute leukemias.
- Hodgkin lymphoma.
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
- Hairy cell leukemia.

![CT in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia showing splenomegaly; the arrows point at the spleen.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/Splenomegalie_bei_CLL_%28labeled%29.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Splenomegalie_bei_CLL_(labeled).jpg; credit=Hellerhoff. Labeling by Mikael Häggström · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY-SA 3.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0; added=yes}

### 3. Myeloproliferative disorders

- Primary myelofibrosis.
- Polycythemia vera.
- Essential thrombocythemia.

## B. Infectious causes

### Acute infections

- Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
- CMV
- Viral hepatitis
- Typhoid fever

### Chronic infections

- Malaria
- Tuberculosis
- Brucellosis
- Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar)
- Infective endocarditis
- Histoplasmosis

## C. Congestive causes

### Increased pressure in the splenic venous circulation

- Portal hypertension.
- Liver cirrhosis.
- Portal vein thrombosis.
- Splenic vein thrombosis.
- Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd–Chiari syndrome).
- Right-sided heart failure (in some cases).

![Abdominal CT showing liver cirrhosis and splenomegaly due to secondary portal hypertension.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d1/Liver_cirrhosis.JPG){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Liver_cirrhosis.JPG; credit=Inversitus · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY-SA 3.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0; added=yes}

## D. Autoimmune and inflammatory causes

- Rheumatoid arthritis.
- Felty syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia).
- Systemic lupus erythematosus.
- Sarcoidosis.
- Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).

## E. Storage and infiltrative diseases

- Gaucher disease.
- Niemann–Pick disease.
- Amyloidosis.
- Glycogen storage diseases.

## F. Local splenic pathology

- Splenic cysts.
- Splenic abscess.
- Splenic tumors.
- Splenic hematoma.
- Splenic infarction (may cause enlargement, particularly in the acute phase).

## How to remember

### Five major mechanisms

- Increased destruction of blood cells.
- Increased blood pooling/congestion.
- Infection and immune stimulation.
- Malignant or infiltrative disease.
- Local structural pathology.

:::reference Reference
Merck Manual Professional Edition +2
:::

title: 4. What are the surgical causes of splenomegaly?
model_answer:
### Overview

This question is slightly different from the general differential diagnosis. In a surgical viva, emphasize conditions involving the spleen itself, its vessels, or adjacent abdominal structures.

### 1. Splenic cysts

- Hydatid cyst.
- Congenital epithelial cyst.
- Post-traumatic pseudocyst.

### 2. Splenic abscess

- Pyogenic abscess.
- Tuberculous abscess (less common).
- Fungal abscess, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

### 3. Splenic tumors

- Primary lymphoma.
- Hemangioma.
- Lymphangioma.
- Angiosarcoma (rare).
- Metastatic tumors (uncommon).

### 4. Splenic vascular disorders

- Splenic vein thrombosis.
- Portal vein thrombosis.
- Splenic artery aneurysm (important surgical differential for a left upper abdominal mass, although it is not a cause of splenomegaly itself).

### 5. Traumatic conditions

- Splenic hematoma.
- Subcapsular hematoma.
- Splenic rupture.
- Splenic infarction following vascular injury.

### 6. Portal hypertension

- Cirrhosis.
- Extrahepatic portal vein obstruction.
- Portal or splenic venous thrombosis.

:::important Important distinction
Splenic rupture, an aneurysm and infarction are important surgical splenic conditions, but they should not all be presented as causes of chronic splenomegaly. An aneurysm, for example, is a separate vascular pathology.
:::

:::reference Reference
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov +3
:::

title: 5. What are the causes of splenic cysts? (important general surgery question)
model_answer:
### Classification

Splenic cysts are classified according to the presence or absence of an epithelial lining.

### A. True cysts (primary cysts)

Have an epithelial lining.

### 1. Parasitic cysts

- Hydatid cyst caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

:::note Note
Particularly important in Iraq and other endemic regions.
:::

### 2. Non-parasitic cysts

- Congenital cysts.
- Epidermoid cysts.
- Dermoid cysts (rare).

### B. False cysts (secondary cysts / pseudocysts)

Lack an epithelial lining. Causes include:
- Trauma – the most important cause.
- Previous splenic hematoma.
- Splenic infarction.
- Previous splenic abscess or inflammation.
- Hemorrhage into the splenic parenchyma.

![CT of a splenic pseudocyst with typical rim calcification and no septation.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Pseudozyste_der_Milz_43M_-_CT_axial_coronar_-_001.jpg/960px-Pseudozyste_der_Milz_43M_-_CT_axial_coronar_-_001.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pseudozyste_der_Milz_43M_-_CT_axial_coronar_-_001.jpg; credit=Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY-SA 4.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0; added=yes}

| Comparison | True cyst | Pseudocyst |
|---|---|---|
| Epithelial lining | Present | Absent |
| Main causes | Congenital, parasitic | Trauma, hematoma, infarction |
| Hydatid disease | Yes | No |
| Wall | Variable | Often fibrous and may calcify |

:::tip Exam question: Why is a post-traumatic splenic cyst called a pseudocyst?
Because it lacks an epithelial lining. It develops when a hematoma within the spleen fails to resolve completely and becomes surrounded by a fibrous wall.
:::

:::tip Additional viva question: Most important parasitic cause?
Hydatid disease caused by Echinococcus granulosus.
:::

:::reference Reference
PubMed Central (PMC) +3
:::

title: Q6. Why doesn't the spleen descend into the left iliac fossa?
model_answer:
:::group
Q6–Q7. Why doesn't the spleen descend into the left iliac fossa? Role of the phrenicocolic ligament
:::

This question tests your understanding of the supporting ligaments of the spleen. The spleen is normally located in the left hypochondrium, beneath the left hemidiaphragm.

![Lateral view of the thorax showing the position of the spleen (Gray's Anatomy, fig. 1217).](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/72/Gray1217.png){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray1217.png; credit=Henry Vandyke Carter · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons; license=Public domain; added=yes}

### Peritoneal ligaments holding the spleen

- Gastrosplenic ligament: connects the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach. Contains short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels.
- Splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament: connects the spleen to the left kidney. Contains the splenic vessels and tail of the pancreas.
- Phrenicocolic ligament: connects the left colic flexure to the diaphragm and supports the spleen from below.
- Phrenicosplenic ligament: a variable peritoneal attachment to the diaphragm.

The spleen is also supported by its relationship with the diaphragm and surrounding structures.

![Horizontal disposition of the peritoneum in the upper part of the abdomen (Gray's Anatomy, fig. 1039).](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Gray1039.png){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gray1039.png; credit=Henry Vandyke Carter · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons; license=Public domain; added=yes}

### The main answer

The spleen does not normally descend into the left iliac fossa because it is supported by its peritoneal attachments, particularly the phrenicocolic ligament, which acts as a shelf beneath it.

### Why can a massively enlarged spleen reach the pelvis?

Because the spleen enlarges downwards and medially, following the path of least resistance in the abdomen. Its supporting attachments do not prevent pathological enlargement; they simply provide anatomical support. This explains why an enlarged spleen can extend towards the umbilicus, right iliac fossa or even the pelvis.

title: Q7. Role of the phrenicocolic ligament
model_answer:
:::group
Q6–Q7. Why doesn't the spleen descend into the left iliac fossa? Role of the phrenicocolic ligament
:::

:::definition Definition
A peritoneal fold extending from the left colic flexure (splenic flexure) of the colon to the diaphragm. It lies inferior to the spleen.
:::

### Functions

1. Supports the spleen – its most important function is providing a shelf-like support beneath the spleen.
2. Prevents excessive downward displacement – helps maintain the spleen in its normal anatomical position in the left hypochondrium.
3. Supports the left colic flexure – maintains the relationship between the splenic flexure and the diaphragm.

### Alternative name (high-yield viva fact)

Sustentaculum lienis = support of the spleen. The term comes from its function as a supporting shelf beneath the spleen.

### Clinical relevance

- It is an important anatomical support of the spleen.
- Its laxity or absence may contribute to abnormal splenic mobility.
- A wandering spleen is associated with abnormal or lax suspensory ligaments, which can predispose to torsion of the splenic pedicle.

:::reference Reference
IMAIOS +3 (Q6); IMAIOS +1 (Q7)
:::

title: 1. Mechanism of splenic injury
model_answer:
### Overview

The spleen is the most commonly injured intra-abdominal organ in blunt abdominal trauma.

It is particularly vulnerable because:
- It is highly vascular.
- It has a relatively thin capsule.
- It is situated beneath the left lower ribs.
- It is relatively fixed by its supporting ligaments.
- It has a soft, friable parenchyma.

### A. Blunt abdominal trauma

This is the most common mechanism.

Examples:
- Road traffic accidents.
- Falls from height.
- Direct blows to the left upper abdomen.
- Sports injuries.
- Assaults.
- Compression of the abdomen against the spine.

### Mechanism of injury (blunt)

- Direct impact causes compression of the spleen against the posterior abdominal wall or lower ribs.
- Sudden deceleration produces shearing forces at the splenic attachments and vascular pedicle.
- The splenic parenchyma tears.
- The capsule may rupture.
- Blood escapes into the peritoneal cavity, causing hemoperitoneum.

### Other possible injuries

- Splenic laceration.
- Subcapsular hematoma.
- Intraparenchymal hematoma.
- Vascular pedicle injury.
- Complete splenic rupture.

### B. Penetrating abdominal trauma

Examples:
- Stab wounds.
- Gunshot wounds.
- Penetrating fragments from explosions.

The penetrating object directly damages the splenic capsule, parenchyma or vessels. Gunshot wounds may cause more extensive injury because of the projectile's energy and trajectory.

### C. Iatrogenic injury

Splenic injury may occur during abdominal operations, particularly:
- Gastric surgery.
- Colonic surgery, especially splenic flexure mobilization.
- Pancreatic surgery.
- Left upper abdominal procedures.

Traction on the splenocolic or gastrosplenic attachments can cause capsular tears.

### D. Spontaneous or pathological splenic rupture

Occurs without significant trauma or following minimal trauma in a diseased spleen.

Predisposing conditions include:
- Infectious mononucleosis (EBV).
- Malaria.
- Hematological malignancies, particularly leukemia and lymphoma.
- Myeloproliferative disorders.
- Splenic infarction.
- Splenic tumors.
- Certain infiltrative diseases.

![Splenomegaly due to infectious mononucleosis resulting in a subcapsular haematoma (CT, marked).](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/33/SplenomegalyandsubcaphematomaMarked.png){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SplenomegalyandsubcaphematomaMarked.png; credit=James Heilman, MD · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY-SA 4.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0; added=yes}

:::tip Viva distinction
A normal spleen can rupture following significant trauma, whereas a pathological spleen may rupture spontaneously or following relatively minor trauma.
:::

### Types of anatomical injury

- Subcapsular hematoma: Blood collects beneath the splenic capsule
- Intraparenchymal hematoma: Blood collects within splenic tissue
- Laceration: Tear in splenic parenchyma
- Capsular rupture: Disruption of the splenic capsule
- Vascular injury: Damage to splenic vessels
- Shattered spleen: Extensive destruction of splenic tissue
- Hilar injury: Damage to vessels entering or leaving the spleen

:::important Important concept: Delayed splenic rupture
A patient may initially appear stable following trauma and develop hemorrhage hours or days later.

This can occur when:
- An initially contained subcapsular hematoma expands.
- A hematoma ruptures into the peritoneal cavity.
- A vascular lesion, such as a pseudoaneurysm, ruptures.

Therefore, an initially stable patient does not necessarily have a harmless splenic injury.
:::

title: 2. Modes of presentation
model_answer:
### A. Acute presentation

Classical presentation following blunt or penetrating abdominal trauma.

Symptoms:
- Left upper quadrant abdominal pain.
- Generalized abdominal pain if there is significant hemoperitoneum.
- Pain referred to the left shoulder (Kehr's sign).
- Dizziness or fainting.
- Weakness.
- Nausea and vomiting.
- Symptoms of hypovolemia or hemorrhagic shock.

Clinical picture: a patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with left upper quadrant pain, tachycardia, pallor, abdominal tenderness, and hypotension if significant blood loss has occurred.

### B. Delayed presentation

The patient may initially be stable and present later with:
- Increasing abdominal pain.
- Abdominal distension.
- Dizziness.
- Syncope.
- Tachycardia.
- Hypotension.
- Features of delayed intraperitoneal hemorrhage.

Delayed rupture is an important reason for observation and follow-up in selected patients.

### C. Presentation with hemorrhagic shock (surgical emergency)

Severe splenic hemorrhage can cause hypovolemic shock.

Features include:
- Tachycardia.
- Hypotension.
- Cold, clammy extremities.
- Pallor.
- Sweating.
- Altered mental status.
- Delayed capillary refill.
- Reduced urine output.
- Weak peripheral pulses.

:::important Important
Hypotension is a late sign in many patients, particularly young adults who can compensate for considerable blood loss.
:::

### D. Occult or minimally symptomatic presentation

Some patients have a relatively small splenic injury and may have:
- Mild left upper quadrant tenderness.
- Normal vital signs.
- No obvious abdominal distension.
- No significant initial fall in hemoglobin.

These patients may be diagnosed incidentally on imaging performed after trauma.

### E. Spontaneous rupture presentation

The patient may have no history of trauma and present with:
- Sudden left upper quadrant pain.
- Left shoulder pain.
- Abdominal distension.
- Collapse.
- Hemodynamic instability.

The examiner may ask you to consider spontaneous rupture in a patient with infectious mononucleosis or hematological malignancy.

title: 3. Physical signs of splenic injury
model_answer:
### Overview

The physical examination is important, but remember that a normal abdominal examination does not exclude splenic injury. Some patients have minimal signs initially, particularly in the early stages of hemorrhage.

## A. General examination (look for blood loss and shock)

| Sign / Finding | Details |
|---|---|
| Pallor | Blood loss |
| Tachycardia | Compensatory response to hypovolemia |
| Hypotension | Significant blood loss or decompensated shock |
| Cold, clammy skin | Peripheral vasoconstriction |
| Tachypnea | Compensation for shock |
| Altered consciousness | Reduced cerebral perfusion |
| Delayed capillary refill | Peripheral hypoperfusion |
| Reduced urine output | Reduced renal perfusion |

## B. Local abdominal examination

### 1. Inspection

Look for:
- Abdominal distension.
- Bruising over the left upper quadrant.
- Seatbelt sign.
- Abrasions.
- Penetrating wounds.
- Associated lower left rib injuries.

### 2. Palpation

Findings include:
- Left upper quadrant tenderness.
- Generalized abdominal tenderness.
- Guarding.
- Rigidity.
- Rebound tenderness.
- Abdominal wall tenderness.

Guarding and rigidity may indicate peritoneal irritation due to intraperitoneal blood.

### 3. Percussion

- Generalized abdominal dullness may occur with significant hemoperitoneum.
- Flank dullness may be present.
- Shifting dullness may occur when a substantial amount of free intraperitoneal blood accumulates.

### 4. Auscultation

Bowel sounds may be reduced or absent due to ileus associated with peritoneal irritation.

## C. Examination of the chest

:::important Important – associated lower left rib fractures
Look for:
- Tenderness over the left lower ribs (particularly ribs 9–12).
- Bruising.
- Crepitus.
- Rib fractures.
- Reduced air entry if an associated thoracic injury exists.
:::

:::pearl Exam pearl
Left lower rib fractures following trauma should raise suspicion of an underlying splenic injury.
:::

## D. Other associated signs

- Left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign).
- Left flank findings (Ballance's sign).
- Signs of associated pancreatic, renal, bowel or diaphragmatic injury.

:::reference Reference
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov +2
:::

title: 4. Kehr's sign
model_answer:
:::group
Q4–Q5. Kehr's sign and Ballance's sign
:::

:::definition Definition (very important viva question)
Referred pain to the left shoulder caused by irritation of the diaphragm due to blood or other irritating material in the peritoneal cavity. Classically associated with splenic rupture.
:::

### Mechanism

- Splenic injury causes bleeding.
- Blood accumulates in the peritoneal cavity (hemoperitoneum).
- Blood irritates the undersurface of the diaphragm.
- The phrenic nerve is stimulated.
- Pain is referred to the shoulder.

### Why shoulder pain?

The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4, C5. It supplies sensory innervation to the central diaphragm.

The same cervical spinal cord segments receive sensory input from the shoulder region, particularly through the supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4). Therefore, the brain interprets diaphragmatic irritation as shoulder pain.

![Referred pain chart: visceral sensations are perceived over characteristic regions of the body surface.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/1506_Referred_Pain_Chart.jpg/960px-1506_Referred_Pain_Chart.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1506_Referred_Pain_Chart.jpg; credit=OpenStax College · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY 3.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0; added=yes}

:::remember Remember
C3, C4, C5 keep the diaphragm alive.
:::

### Clinical significance

- Suggests diaphragmatic irritation.
- Can be associated with splenic rupture.
- Usually involves the left shoulder in splenic injury.
- May be more noticeable with inspiration.

:::important Important
Kehr's sign is suggestive, not diagnostic. Its absence does not exclude splenic rupture.
:::

:::tip Examiner follow-up: Can Kehr's sign occur in other conditions?
Yes. It can occur in any condition causing diaphragmatic irritation, including:
- Hemoperitoneum from other causes.
- Ectopic pregnancy with intraperitoneal bleeding.
- Subphrenic abscess.
- Other causes of diaphragmatic irritation.
:::

:::reference Reference
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov +2
:::

title: 5. Ballance's sign
model_answer:
:::group
Q4–Q5. Kehr's sign and Ballance's sign
:::

:::definition Definition
A clinical finding associated with splenic rupture, characterized by:
- Persistent dullness in the left flank.
- Shifting dullness in the right flank.
:::

### Mechanism

Explained by the different behavior of clotted and free blood in the peritoneal cavity.

Left flank: Blood accumulates around the injured spleen. Some blood clots locally. The clotted blood remains relatively fixed. Therefore, dullness persists in the left flank even when the patient changes position.

Right flank: Blood that remains liquid flows freely within the peritoneal cavity. When the patient changes position, free blood shifts. Therefore, the area of dullness changes.

### How do you demonstrate it?

- Percuss the left flank with the patient supine.
- Change the patient's position.
- Percuss again.
- The dullness on the left remains relatively fixed.
- The right flank demonstrates shifting dullness.

### Why is it important?

It is a classical historical sign suggesting splenic rupture with hemoperitoneum.

### Kehr's vs Ballance's

- Kehr's: Left shoulder pain | Referred pain | Diaphragmatic irritation | Phrenic nerve
- Ballance's: Fixed left flank dullness | Percussion finding | Clotted versus free intraperitoneal blood | Blood distribution

:::tip Viva answer to memorize
"Ballance's sign is fixed dullness in the left flank due to localized clotted blood, with shifting dullness in the right flank due to free intraperitoneal blood."

It is a classical sign and is not sufficiently sensitive or specific to guide modern trauma management.
:::

title: 6. Management of splenic injury
model_answer:
## Key principle

### Potentially life-threatening hemorrhage

Hemodynamic status determines the initial management, not the CT injury grade alone.

Goals:
- Control hemorrhage.
- Restore circulating blood volume and tissue perfusion.
- Preserve the spleen whenever safely possible.
- Prevent delayed hemorrhage and other complications.
- Identify associated injuries.

## A. Initial assessment – ATLS (ABCDE)

### A – Airway with cervical spine protection

- Assess airway patency.
- Protect the cervical spine when indicated.
- Secure the airway if necessary.

### B – Breathing

- Assess respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and chest movement.
- Look for associated thoracic trauma.
- Treat life-threatening chest injuries.

### C – Circulation with hemorrhage control

Particularly important in splenic injury.
- Assess pulse and blood pressure.
- Establish two large-bore IV lines.
- Send blood for investigations and crossmatching.
- Begin appropriate blood product resuscitation if hemorrhagic shock is suspected.
- Activate the massive transfusion protocol when indicated.
- Monitor for ongoing bleeding.

Avoid relying on large volumes of crystalloid when major hemorrhage is present.

### D – Disability

- Assess Glasgow Coma Scale.
- Check pupils.
- Assess neurological status.

### E – Exposure

- Fully expose the patient to identify other injuries.
- Prevent hypothermia.

## Initial investigations

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| CBC | Hemoglobin, hematocrit and platelet count |
| Blood group and crossmatch | Prepare for transfusion |
| Coagulation profile | Assess coagulopathy |
| Urea and electrolytes | Baseline renal and metabolic assessment |
| ABG/VBG | Assess perfusion, lactate and base deficit |
| FAST/eFAST | Detect free intraperitoneal fluid |
| Contrast-enhanced CT | Identify and grade splenic injury in stable patients |

## B. Imaging

### 1. FAST scan

FAST = Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma.

Looks for free fluid in the:
- Pericardial space.
- Right upper quadrant (hepatorenal recess).
- Left upper quadrant (splenorenal recess).
- Pelvis.

Advantages: rapid, bedside, non-invasive, useful in unstable trauma patients.

A positive FAST in an unstable patient with suspected intra-abdominal bleeding supports urgent operative management. A negative FAST does not exclude splenic injury.

### 2. Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen (gold standard in hemodynamically stable patients)

CT helps identify:
- Splenic lacerations.
- Hematomas.
- Hemoperitoneum.
- Active contrast extravasation (contrast blush).
- Splenic pseudoaneurysm.
- Vascular injury.
- Associated abdominal injuries.

The CT findings help determine whether observation, angioembolization or surgery is appropriate.

:::reference Reference
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov +2
:::

## C. AAST grading

See the AAST Grading sheet.

## D. Management decision: Stable versus unstable (probably the most important part of the whole topic)

### Algorithm

Patient with suspected splenic injury → ATLS primary survey and resuscitation → Assess hemodynamic status

### UNSTABLE

Persistent shock or transient response with suspected ongoing bleeding → Urgent laparotomy → Hemorrhage control, usually splenectomy when necessary

### STABLE

Maintains perfusion after assessment/resuscitation → Contrast CT → Grade injury and identify vascular lesions.

Stable patient:
- No ongoing bleeding or vascular lesion: Non-operative management.
- Active bleeding, contrast blush or pseudoaneurysm: Consider splenic artery embolization.
- Failure of non-operative management or another indication for laparotomy: Surgery.

:::important One critical point
A patient with a grade IV or V injury can sometimes be managed without surgery if hemodynamically stable, with appropriate interventional radiology support. Conversely, a patient with a grade I injury who remains in hemorrhagic shock needs urgent hemorrhage control.
:::

:::reference Reference
Practice Management Guideline +3
:::

title: AAST grading of splenic injury (five grades)
model_answer:
:::note Note
The American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) classifies splenic injuries into five grades. Important because it helps assess injury severity and plan management.
:::

| Grade | Description |
|---|---|
| I | Subcapsular hematoma less than 10% of surface area; laceration less than 1 cm deep |
| II | Subcapsular hematoma 10–50%; intraparenchymal hematoma less than 5 cm; laceration 1–3 cm deep |
| III | Subcapsular hematoma greater than 50% or expanding; intraparenchymal hematoma at least 5 cm or expanding; laceration greater than 3 cm |
| IV | Splenic vascular injury or active bleeding confined within the splenic capsule; or segmental/hilar vascular injury causing more than 25% devascularization |
| V | Shattered spleen or vascular injury with active bleeding extending beyond the spleen into the peritoneal cavity |

:::note Update
The 2018 AAST revision includes vascular injuries and active bleeding in the grading criteria. Older textbooks may describe grades IV and V differently.
:::

:::reference Reference
AAST 2018 Spleen Injury Scale – University of Washington
:::

title: 7. Conservative (non-operative) management of splenic injury – in detail (very high-yield viva topic)
model_answer:
:::definition Definition
Conservative management is also called non-operative management (NOM). It means treating splenic injury without immediate surgical removal of the spleen. It has become the preferred approach for most hemodynamically stable patients with blunt splenic injury.
:::

### A. Indications

The most important indication is hemodynamic stability.

Other considerations:
- No generalized peritonitis.
- No other abdominal injury requiring laparotomy.
- Ability to monitor the patient closely.
- Availability of blood products.
- Immediate access to an operating theatre if deterioration occurs.
- Access to interventional radiology when embolization is required.

Can be used in: Grade I, II, III injuries, and selected grade IV and V injuries.

:::important Important
The grade alone does not determine whether conservative treatment is possible.
:::

### B. Contraindications / reasons to abandon

- Persistent hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation.
- Persistent or recurrent hemorrhagic shock.
- Generalized peritonitis.
- Another intra-abdominal injury requiring operative treatment.
- Failure of non-operative management.
- Inability to provide adequate monitoring and urgent intervention.

A high AAST grade, large hemoperitoneum or contrast blush is not automatically a contraindication to a non-operative approach in a stable patient, but these findings may make embolization necessary.

### C. How is it performed?

Go through it as if you are managing the patient in the hospital.

:::step 1 Hospital admission
The patient should be admitted to an appropriately monitored trauma or surgical unit.
- Low-grade injuries may be monitored on a surgical ward if staffing and observation are adequate.
- High-grade injuries generally require a high-dependency unit (HDU) or intensive care unit (ICU), depending on clinical condition.
:::

:::step 2 Close hemodynamic monitoring
- Blood pressure: detect hypotension
- Heart rate: detect tachycardia
- Respiratory rate: detect deterioration
- Oxygen saturation: monitor oxygenation
- Temperature: detect hypothermia or infection
- Urine output: assess renal perfusion
- Mental status: detect reduced cerebral perfusion
- Abdominal examination: detect increasing tenderness or distension

Urine output is particularly useful in assessing perfusion. Typical adult target: ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
:::

:::step 3 Serial laboratory investigations
CBC and hemoglobin monitoring:
- Check initial hemoglobin and hematocrit.
- Repeat measurements according to the injury grade and clinical status.
- Look for a progressive fall suggesting ongoing bleeding.

A normal initial hemoglobin does not exclude major acute hemorrhage because equilibration takes time.

Other investigations may include: platelet count, coagulation profile, lactate, base deficit, renal function.
:::

:::step 4 Bed rest and mobilization
Older protocols recommended prolonged bed rest. Current evidence supports earlier mobilization in stable patients.

2022 WSES consensus:
- Grade I–II: Within 24 hours
- Grade III: Around 48 hours
- Grade IV–V: Around 48 hours if clinically stable and serial hemoglobin measurements are stable

For high-grade injuries, the WSES consensus suggests that three successive hemoglobin measurements, taken 8 hours apart after the first, should remain within 10% of one another before mobilization.

These are guideline suggestions, not rigid rules; associated injuries and clinical condition matter.
:::

:::step 5 Fluid and blood replacement
- Establish IV access.
- Give appropriate resuscitation.
- Use blood products when indicated by hemorrhage and clinical status.
- Correct coagulopathy, hypothermia and hypocalcemia when present.
- Avoid unnecessary crystalloid administration.

Do not use a normal blood pressure after transient resuscitation as proof that bleeding has stopped.
:::

:::step 6 Analgesia
- Paracetamol may be used.
- Opioids may be required for severe pain.
- Avoid masking clinical deterioration with inadequate reassessment.
:::

:::step 7 Repeat imaging
Not required routinely for every patient. However, important in selected high-grade injuries and when vascular complications are suspected.

The 2022 WSES consensus suggests contrast-enhanced CT or contrast-enhanced ultrasound at approximately 48–72 hours in patients with AAST grade III or higher managed non-operatively.

Particularly important if there is:
- New or increasing abdominal pain.
- Tachycardia.
- A fall in hemoglobin.
- New hypotension.
- Suspected pseudoaneurysm.
- Suspected delayed bleeding.
:::

:::step 8 Splenic artery angioembolization
Definition: Splenic artery embolization (SAE) is an interventional radiological procedure in which the splenic artery or its branches are occluded to control bleeding while preserving viable splenic tissue.

Indications:
- Active contrast extravasation (arterial blush) on CT.
- Splenic artery pseudoaneurysm.
- Arteriovenous fistula.
- Selected high-grade splenic injuries.
- Persistent concern for bleeding in a stable patient.
:::

### WSES 2022 on SAE

- SAE is recommended as a first-line intervention in hemodynamically stable patients with arterial blush, irrespective of injury grade, when resources are available.
- Angiography and possible embolization are suggested for stable adults with grade IV–V injuries, even without a visible blush, in appropriately equipped centers.
- Grade III injuries without blush require individualized assessment, particularly when risk factors for failure are present.

### Types of embolization

- Proximal embolization: Occludes the main splenic artery, reducing perfusion pressure while maintaining collateral blood supply.
- Distal embolization: Occludes a specific bleeding branch.

The WSES consensus suggests preferring proximal embolization when SAE is needed, although the choice depends on the vascular anatomy and clinical situation.

### E. Advantages of conservative management

- Preserves splenic function.
- Reduces the need for splenectomy.
- Avoids lifelong increased risk of overwhelming postsplenectomy infection.
- Avoids some complications of major abdominal surgery.
- Allows preservation of the spleen's immunological function.

### F. Complications / causes of failure (know for the viva)

1. Delayed hemorrhage: rebleeding after initial stabilization.
2. Delayed splenic rupture: a previously contained injury ruptures into the peritoneal cavity.
3. Splenic artery pseudoaneurysm: a vascular injury that can rupture and cause significant hemorrhage.
4. Arteriovenous fistula: an abnormal communication between an artery and vein.
5. Splenic infarction: loss of blood supply to part of the spleen.
6. Splenic abscess: may occur following infarction or infection.
7. Failure of non-operative management: persistent bleeding or hemodynamic deterioration requiring intervention or surgery.

:::reference Reference
PubMed Central (PMC) +4
:::

title: 8. When do you convert from conservative management to surgery?
model_answer:
:::group
8–9. Conversion to surgery; operative management
:::

Very important viva question. You abandon conservative management if the patient develops:
- Persistent hypotension despite adequate resuscitation.
- Recurrent hemorrhagic shock.
- Progressive tachycardia with evidence of ongoing bleeding.
- Progressive hemoglobin decline associated with ongoing hemorrhage.
- Increasing hemoperitoneum with clinical deterioration.
- Generalized peritonitis.
- Failure of embolization or other non-operative interventions.
- Another abdominal injury requiring laparotomy.

:::remember Remember
A falling hemoglobin alone does not automatically mean splenectomy. Interpret it alongside vital signs, transfusion requirements, imaging and the overall clinical picture.
:::

title: 9. Operative management – indications
model_answer:
:::group
8–9. Conversion to surgery; operative management
:::

When non-operative management is inappropriate or fails, surgery is required.
- Hemodynamic instability due to splenic hemorrhage.
- Persistent active bleeding.
- Generalized peritonitis or associated injury requiring laparotomy.
- Failed conservative management.
- Failed or unavailable embolization when hemorrhage requires operative control.

### A. Splenectomy

Complete removal of the spleen. Particularly appropriate in:
- Shattered spleen.
- Extensive hilar injury.
- Uncontrollable hemorrhage.
- Severe injury where preservation is not feasible.

### B. Splenorrhaphy

Repair of the injured spleen to preserve splenic tissue. Methods include:
- Suturing of capsular tears.
- Hemostatic materials.
- Topical hemostatic agents.
- Selected tissue-preserving techniques.

### C. Partial splenectomy

Removal of the injured portion while preserving viable splenic tissue. Considered in selected injuries where technically feasible.

### What happens after splenectomy?

The patient becomes functionally asplenic and is at increased risk of overwhelming postsplenectomy infection (OPSI).

Important organisms:
- Streptococcus pneumoniae.
- Haemophilus influenzae type b.
- Neisseria meningitidis.

Prevention includes:
- Appropriate vaccinations.
- Education about seeking urgent medical care for fever.
- Antibiotic prophylaxis according to local protocols and patient risk.

:::reference Reference
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov +2
:::

title: 10. Discharge and follow-up after conservative management
model_answer:
:::tip Examiner question
"Can you send the patient home after conservative treatment?" Yes, once the patient is clinically stable and meets appropriate discharge criteria.
:::

### Discharge criteria

- Hemodynamically stable.
- No evidence of ongoing hemorrhage.
- Stable hemoglobin.
- Adequate pain control.
- Tolerating oral intake.
- Mobilizing safely.
- No associated injury requiring continued admission.
- Appropriate follow-up and patient education arranged.

### Activity restriction (2022 WSES consensus)

- Grade I–II: 3–5 weeks
- Grade III–V: 2–4 months

Suggested restriction of major physical activities. These include heavy lifting, athletic activity and contact sports. Follow-up imaging may be considered before returning to full activity, especially after high-grade injury.

### Patient education – return immediately if

- Sudden or increasing abdominal pain.
- Left shoulder pain.
- Dizziness or fainting.
- Weakness.
- Pallor.
- Palpitations.
- Collapse.

These may indicate delayed hemorrhage or rupture.

:::reference Reference
PubMed Central (PMC) +1
:::

title: 11. Complications of splenic injury (a useful final viva question)
model_answer:
### Early complications

- Hemorrhagic shock.
- Hemoperitoneum.
- Peritonitis.
- Associated pancreatic or bowel injury.
- Death from uncontrolled hemorrhage.

### Late complications

- Delayed splenic rupture.
- Delayed hemorrhage.
- Splenic artery pseudoaneurysm.
- Arteriovenous fistula.
- Splenic infarction.
- Splenic abscess.
- Pseudocyst formation.
- Postsplenectomy overwhelming infection.

title: Overview — Hydatid cyst of the spleen
model_answer:
## Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

:::pearl Key point
The most important distinction to understand is that the hydatid cyst has three layers, but only two are produced by the parasite. This is a frequent question.
:::

### Sheet guide

- 1. Definition & Organism (Q1–Q2)
- 2. Life Cycle (Q3)
- 3. Hosts (Q4–Q5)
- 4. Cyst Layers (Q6)
- 5. Sites (Q7–Q8)
- 6. Treatment (Q9)
- 7. Splenic Treatment (Q10)
- 8. Viva Q&A (Q11)
- 9. WHO Stages
- 10. References (13)
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q1. Define hydatid cyst
model_answer:
:::group
Q1–Q2. Define hydatid cyst; causative organism
:::

A hydatid cyst is a fluid-filled parasitic cyst caused by the larval (metacestode) stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus.

It develops in the organs of an intermediate host following ingestion of parasite eggs.

### The cyst contains

- Hydatid fluid.
- Germinal membrane.
- Brood capsules.
- Daughter cysts.
- Protoscolices (hydatid sand).

It commonly affects the liver and lungs, but can develop in almost any organ.

![Fluid from a hydatid cyst showing “hydatid sand” (Echinococcus granulosus).](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Contents_of_Echinococcus_%28hydatid%29_cyst_Case_192_%285998593961%29.jpg/960px-Contents_of_Echinococcus_%28hydatid%29_cyst_Case_192_%285998593961%29.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Contents_of_Echinococcus_(hydatid)_cyst_Case_192_(5998593961).jpg; credit=Yale Rosen from USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY-SA 2.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0; added=yes}

:::important Important
Hydatid disease is also called cystic echinococcosis.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q2. Causative organism
model_answer:
:::group
Q1–Q2. Define hydatid cyst; causative organism
:::

Most important: Echinococcus granulosus.

It is a small cestode (tapeworm) belonging to the family Taeniidae.

For the classical surgical hydatid cyst question, the expected answer is Echinococcus granulosus.

### Other species of medical importance

- Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato → Cystic echinococcosis
- Echinococcus multilocularis → Alveolar echinococcosis
- Echinococcus vogeli → Polycystic echinococcosis
- Echinococcus oligarthrus → Polycystic echinococcosis

### Morphology of the adult worm

- Is approximately 3–6 mm long.
- Lives in the small intestine of dogs and other canids.
- Has a scolex with four suckers.
- Has a rostellum with hooks.
- Usually has three proglottids: immature, mature and gravid.

The gravid segment contains eggs that are passed in the dog's feces.
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q3. Explain the life cycle of Echinococcus granulosus
model_answer:
### Overview

One of the most important questions in the topic. You should be able to explain it in sequence and draw it if requested.

Two main hosts:
- Definitive host: dog.
- Intermediate host: sheep and other herbivores.

:::step 1 Adult worm in the dog
The adult Echinococcus granulosus lives in the small intestine of the dog. The gravid segments release eggs, which are passed into the environment through the dog's feces.
:::

:::step 2 Contamination of the environment
The eggs contaminate:
- Soil.
- Grass.
- Water.
- Vegetables.
- Food.
:::

:::step 3 Ingestion by the intermediate host
Sheep ingest the eggs while grazing on contaminated grass or food.

Humans can also accidentally ingest eggs through contaminated food, water or hands.
:::

:::step 4 Hatching in the intestine
The eggs reach the small intestine and release the oncosphere (hexacanth embryo). The oncosphere penetrates the intestinal mucosa and enters the portal circulation.
:::

:::step 5 Migration to organs
The oncospheres travel through the bloodstream. The liver acts as the first major filtering organ, followed by the lungs. Some embryos pass through both filters and reach other organs.
:::

:::step 6 Formation of hydatid cyst
Once lodged in an organ, the oncosphere develops into a hydatid cyst. The cyst gradually enlarges and produces:
- Germinal membrane.
- Brood capsules.
- Protoscolices.
- Daughter cysts.
:::

:::step 7 Completion of the cycle
When a dog eats infected sheep viscera containing fertile hydatid cysts, the protoscolices evaginate, attach to the intestinal mucosa and develop into adult tapeworms. The cycle then repeats.
:::

:::remember Remember the cycle
Dog (definitive host): adult worm in small intestine → eggs in feces
↓
Eggs contaminate grass, soil and water
↓
Sheep (intermediate host): ingests eggs → oncosphere → hydatid cyst in organs
↓
Dog eats infected sheep viscera
↓
Dog: protoscolices develop into adult worms

Human = accidental intermediate host: ingests eggs → hydatid cyst develops, but the cycle usually stops here.
:::

![Life cycle of Echinococcus granulosus (CDC).](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Echinococcus_gran_LifeCycle_lg.jpg/960px-Echinococcus_gran_LifeCycle_lg.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Echinococcus_gran_LifeCycle_lg.jpg; credit=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons; license=Public domain; added=yes}

:::pearl Crucial viva point
Humans acquire the infection by ingesting eggs, not by eating infected meat. Eating infected sheep viscera is how dogs become infected.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q4. Definitive host
model_answer:
:::group
Q4–Q5. Definitive and intermediate hosts; why humans are accidental hosts
:::

The dog (Canis familiaris) is the classical definitive host.

Other canids include:
- Wolves.
- Foxes.
- Jackals.

Why called definitive? Because the adult, sexually mature tapeworm lives in their small intestine and produces eggs.

### Intermediate host

The classical intermediate host is the sheep.

Other intermediate hosts include:
- Goats.
- Cattle.
- Camels.
- Pigs.
- Other herbivores.

Why called intermediate? Because the parasite develops into its larval stage (hydatid cyst) inside their organs.

### What about humans?

Humans are accidental (aberrant) intermediate hosts.

:::reference Reference
who.int +2
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q5. Why are humans considered an accidental host?
model_answer:
:::group
Q4–Q5. Definitive and intermediate hosts; why humans are accidental hosts
:::

Three important points:
- Humans accidentally ingest parasite eggs from contaminated food, water, soil or hands.
- The eggs develop into larval hydatid cysts in human organs, just as they do in sheep.
- Humans are not normally eaten by dogs, so the parasite cannot complete its life cycle.

Therefore, humans are considered a dead-end host.

:::important Important viva distinction
Humans do not acquire hydatid disease by eating infected sheep meat.

Transmission routes:
- Sheep → dog: Dog eats infected sheep viscera containing hydatid cysts.
- Dog → human: Human ingests eggs contaminating food, water or hands through dog feces.
- Human → dog: Not part of the normal transmission cycle.
:::

:::reference Reference
who.int +1
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q6. What are the layers of a hydatid cyst? (outside to inside)
model_answer:
### 1. Pericyst (Adventitial layer)

**Origin:** Host · **Main function:** Fibrous protective reaction

- Outermost layer.
- Formed by the host's tissue reaction to the parasite.
- Consists of fibrous connective tissue, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells.
- Not a true parasitic layer.
- Provides a protective fibrous capsule around the cyst.

Remember: This layer is produced by the host.

### 2. Ectocyst (Laminated membrane)

**Origin:** Parasite · **Main function:** Protection and nutrient exchange

- Middle layer.
- Produced by the parasite.
- Acellular, laminated and elastic.
- Semipermeable membrane.
- Allows nutrients to pass from the host to the parasite.
- Provides protection to the parasite.

![Laminated layer of a hydatid cyst, with its “tender coconut” appearance.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b5/Hydatid_cyst_1.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hydatid_cyst_1.jpg; credit=Dr. Roshan Nasimudeen · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY-SA 3.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0; added=yes}

### 3. Endocyst (Germinal layer)

**Origin:** Parasite · **Main function:** Produces new parasitic structures

- Innermost layer.
- Living, nucleated layer.
- Responsible for producing: hydatid fluid, brood capsules, protoscolices, daughter cysts.

This is the most biologically active layer.

:::tip Examiner question: Which layers are parasitic?
The ectocyst and endocyst. The pericyst is formed by the host.
:::

### What is hydatid sand?

Free protoscolices, hooklets and brood capsules suspended in the hydatid fluid.

### What are brood capsules?

Small structures arising from the germinal layer, containing developing protoscolices.

![Protoscolex of Echinococcus granulosus from a hydatid cyst.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Echinococcus_granulosus_scolex.jpg/960px-Echinococcus_granulosus_scolex.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Echinococcus_granulosus_scolex.jpg; credit=CDC/Dr. L.L.A. Moore, Jr · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons; license=Public domain; added=yes}

### What are daughter cysts?

Secondary cysts formed from the germinal layer inside the mother cyst. They may give the cyst a characteristic multivesicular or honeycomb appearance.

:::reference Reference
PubMed Central (PMC) +2
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q7. Common sites of hydatid cysts
model_answer:
:::group
Q7–Q8. Common and uncommon sites of hydatid cysts
:::

### Q7 Overview

Hydatid cysts can develop in almost any organ, but their distribution is determined largely by the route of blood circulation.

### 1. Liver – most common

**Frequency / Clinical importance:** Approximately 60–70%

The liver is the first major filtering organ for embryos entering the portal circulation. The right lobe is more frequently affected than the left.

### 2. Lungs – second most common

**Frequency / Clinical importance:** Approximately 20–30%

The lungs are the second major filtering organ. Pulmonary hydatid cysts may cause:
- Cough.
- Chest pain.
- Dyspnea.
- Hemoptysis.
- Cyst rupture into the bronchial tree.

![Hydatid cyst involving liver and lung: trans-diaphragmatic extension of a liver cyst into the lung.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9b/Echinococcus_%28hydatid%29_cyst_involving_liver_and_lung.jpg){page=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Echinococcus_(hydatid)_cyst_involving_liver_and_lung.jpg; credit=Yale Rosen · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons; license=CC BY-SA 2.0; licenseUrl=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0; added=yes}

### 3. Other less common sites

- Spleen.
- Kidneys.
- Brain.
- Bones.
- Heart.
- Muscles.
- Pancreas.
- Peritoneum.
- Pelvic organs.

The exact percentages vary between populations and studies.

:::reference Reference
who.int +3
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q8. Uncommon sites
model_answer:
:::group
Q7–Q8. Common and uncommon sites of hydatid cysts
:::

Examiner may ask you to list unusual locations.

| Site | Clinical importance |
|---|---|
| Brain | May cause raised intracranial pressure and seizures |
| Heart | May cause arrhythmias, rupture or cardiac tamponade |
| Bones | Can cause progressive bone destruction |
| Kidneys | May produce hydatiduria if the cyst communicates with the collecting system |
| Spleen | Can present as a left upper abdominal mass |
| Pancreas | May mimic a pancreatic cystic tumor |
| Muscles | May present as a soft-tissue swelling |
| Thyroid | Very rare |
| Adrenal gland | Very rare |
| Eye | Can cause orbital compression |

### Why is the spleen an uncommon site?

Because most oncospheres are trapped in the liver and lungs during their passage through the portal and pulmonary circulations. Only a small proportion reach the systemic circulation and other organs.

### How does hydatid disease reach the spleen?

Possible routes include:
- Hematogenous spread through the systemic circulation after passing through the liver and lungs.
- Arterial dissemination.
- Secondary peritoneal dissemination following rupture of another abdominal hydatid cyst.

Important: Splenic hydatid disease is rare compared with hepatic and pulmonary hydatidosis.

:::reference Reference
PubMed Central (PMC) +2
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q9. What is the treatment of hydatid cyst?
model_answer:
### Treatment depends on

- The organ involved.
- Cyst size.
- Cyst stage and viability.
- Whether it is complicated or uncomplicated.
- Presence of daughter cysts.
- Patient's general condition.

There are four main treatment strategies for cystic echinococcosis.

### A. Medical – Albendazole

Albendazole is the main antiparasitic drug.

Mechanism:
- Inhibits microtubule formation by binding to parasite beta-tubulin.
- Interferes with glucose uptake.
- Depletes glycogen stores.
- Leads to degeneration and death of the parasite.

Typical dose: 10–15 mg/kg/day. Maximum: 800 mg/day, divided into two doses. Given with a fatty meal to improve absorption.

### Albendazole indications

- Small uncomplicated cysts in selected patients.
- Multiple cysts that are difficult to approach surgically.
- Before and after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence and secondary dissemination.
- Selected patients who are unsuitable for surgery.

Treatment duration depends on the cyst stage, location and treatment strategy. It may range from weeks to several months.

### Albendazole monitoring

- Liver function tests.
- Complete blood count.
- Clinical and radiological response.

### B. Surgical – indications

Surgery is particularly important for:
- Large cysts.
- Complicated cysts.
- Infected cysts.
- Ruptured cysts.
- Cysts causing pressure symptoms.
- Cysts unsuitable for medical or percutaneous management.

### Surgical options

- Cystectomy: removal of the cyst.
- Pericystectomy: removal of the cyst together with its surrounding fibrous capsule, when feasible.
- Partial cystectomy: removal of the accessible portion of the cyst.
- Organ resection when necessary.

:::important Important surgical precautions
- Isolate the operative field to prevent spillage.
- Avoid accidental rupture.
- Use an appropriate scolicidal agent according to the operative protocol.
- Carefully evacuate cyst contents.
- Avoid dissemination of viable protoscolices.
- Look for additional cysts.
:::

### Rupture can cause

- Anaphylactic reaction.
- Secondary hydatidosis.
- Peritoneal dissemination.
- Local recurrence.

### C. PAIR technique (percutaneous)

PAIR stands for:
- P: Puncture.
- A: Aspiration.
- I: Injection of scolicidal agent.
- R: Re-aspiration.

Steps:
- The cyst is punctured under ultrasound or CT guidance.
- Hydatid fluid is aspirated.
- A scolicidal agent is injected.
- After an appropriate contact period, the fluid is re-aspirated.

Examples of scolicidal agents include hypertonic saline and ethanol. PAIR is used for selected hepatic cyst stages, with appropriate precautions.

:::important Important
PAIR is not a routine treatment for splenic hydatid cysts. It requires careful specialist selection because of the risk of leakage, anaphylaxis and dissemination.
:::

### D. Watch and wait

Some inactive, uncomplicated cysts can be managed conservatively with regular ultrasound or other appropriate imaging follow-up. This avoids unnecessary invasive treatment.

:::reference Reference
who.int +2
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q10. Specifically, what is the treatment of hydatid cyst of the spleen?
model_answer:
:::note Context
This is particularly important because the reported examination concerned splenic hydatid disease.
:::

### First-line surgical option

Splenectomy (removal of the spleen) has traditionally been the conventional definitive surgical treatment, particularly in adults with large, multiple or complicated splenic cysts.

### Why splenectomy?

- Removes the infected organ and cyst completely.
- Prevents local recurrence.
- Reduces the risk of cyst rupture and spillage during subsequent manipulation.
- Provides definitive treatment of extensive splenic involvement.

### Other surgical options

Spleen-preserving surgery can be considered in selected patients, particularly children and patients with localized cysts.

Options include:
- Partial splenectomy.
- Partial cystectomy.
- Total cystectomy when feasible.
- Evacuation of cyst contents with appropriate management of the residual cavity.
- Omentopexy to help obliterate the residual cavity.

### Why preserve the spleen?

Because the spleen has important immunological functions.

Splenectomy increases the risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI), particularly from encapsulated organisms:
- Streptococcus pneumoniae.
- Haemophilus influenzae type b.
- Neisseria meningitidis.

Patients undergoing elective splenectomy require appropriate vaccination, education about infection risk and a prevention plan.

### Role of albendazole

Generally used as perioperative antiparasitic therapy, with the duration individualized according to the surgical and infectious disease team's assessment.

:::important Important distinction
The optimal surgical approach to splenic hydatid cysts is not universally agreed upon. Splenectomy is a conventional definitive option, but spleen-preserving surgery is increasingly considered when technically safe.
:::

:::reference References
- Hydatid Cyst of Spleen: A Diagnostic Challenge – PMC.
- Total Splenectomy versus Spleen-Preserving Surgery.
- Splenic-Preserving Surgery in Hydatid Spleen – 2022 study.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

title: Q11. Additional questions Dr. Salah might ask
model_answer:
| Question | Answer | |---|---| | Q1. What is the infective stage for humans? | The embryonated egg containing the oncosphere. | | Q2. What is the infective stage for dogs? | The protoscolex contained within the hydatid cyst of an infected intermediate host. | | Q3. What is an oncosphere? | The six-hooked embryo released from the egg in the small intestine. | | Q4. What is a hydatid thrill? | A classical clinical sign described when tapping a superficial hydatid cyst produces a palpable or audible vibration due to vibrations transmitted by daughter cysts and their membranes. It is uncommon and not a reliable diagnostic sign. | | Q5. What is the most dangerous complication of hydatid cyst rupture? | Anaphylactic shock.

Other complications include secondary dissemination, infection and compression of surrounding structures. | | Q6. How do you diagnose hydatid disease? | - Ultrasound: particularly useful for abdominal cysts and WHO cyst staging.
- CT scan: defines the location, extent, calcification and relationship with surrounding structures.
- MRI: useful in selected cases, especially neurological and complex disease.
- Serology: Echinococcus-specific IgG can support the diagnosis. | | Q7. What is the WHO classification of hydatid cysts? | The WHO-IWGE ultrasound classification (see WHO Stages sheet). | | Q8. What is the difference between primary and secondary hydatid disease? | - Primary: develops following direct infection after ingestion of eggs.
- Secondary: develops following dissemination of viable parasitic material from a ruptured or manipulated primary cyst. | | Q9. Can hydatid disease be transmitted from one human to another? | No. Normal human-to-human transmission does not occur. | | Q10. How can hydatid disease be prevented? | - Regular deworming of dogs.
- Prevent dogs from eating raw infected animal viscera.
- Proper disposal of infected organs at slaughterhouses.
- Handwashing after handling dogs.
- Washing vegetables and food.
- Improving slaughterhouse hygiene.
- Controlling stray dog populations. |
source: Dr. Salah — Hydatid Cyst of the Spleen OSCE workbook

model_answer:
